new_statements.quote: In Khumi, two-member compounds are typically right-headed (if endocentric) and are phonologically distinguished by the treatment of their first (and sometimes second) element. There are various possibilities, but typically, the first element bears less stress than the second and does not show the full array of tonal distinctions found on its last syllable compared to non-compound occurrences of that member; tonal distinctions on the last syllable of the first member are generally reduced to high vs. low, although tone 4 (rising) in compounds sometimes shows a peak delay that bleeds over into a following syllable, altering the tone of that syllable

new_statements.rule_in_words: Khumi is a tone language (five lexical tones; every syllable carries an underlying tone; syllable canon (C(v))C(C)V(N)+tone with toneless/reduced half-syllables in sesquisyllables). The only stress statement located is at compound level: in a two-member compound the second (head) member is the more stressed one and the first member is weaker, with its tones neutralised to a high/low contrast. No rule for stress placement in simple words was found in any snippet or open paper.
new_statements.exceptions: 'There are various possibilities, but typically...' - the first-element reduction is the typical, not the only, pattern; rising tone 4 on a first member can spread its peak into the following syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Compound (two-member) domain, not word or phrase; half-syllables of sesquisyllabic words are written without a vowel and transcribed with a reduced vowel (p'liwng4 [pə1liwŋ4] 'heart'), i.e. the major syllable is the tone-bearing one, but the source is not quoted as calling this stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All Peterson sources describe Bangladesh Khumi (Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bandarban; Peterson 2002 says two mutually intelligible dialects, c. 2,000 speakers at the time), which is the ISO 639-3 cnk / khum1248 variety; Myanmar (Paletwa) Khumi is also cnk. Eastern Khumi Chin [cek] = east2779 is a separate Glottolog language, and the Lemi (Herr 2011) and 'Kanise Khumi' (Tan 2022) theses noted in the earlier scan belong there or need checking; Mro-Khimi [cmr] (Horney 2012) is a different language again. The earlier scan's citation of a Peterson 'Bangladesh Khumi' chapter in Thurgood & LaPolla (2nd ed.) is wrong: Peterson's chapter there is 'Hakha Lai'; the Khumi chapter is in Vittrant & Watkins 2019 (De Gruyter), pp. 12-55.

sources.citation: Peterson, David A. 2010. Khumi elaborate expressions. Himalayan Linguistics 9(1): 81-100. DOI 10.5070/H99123402
sources.note: Silent on stress. Footnote 1 (pp. 81-82) explains the orthography: five underlying tonal distinctions (low checked, high checked, low falling, high falling, rising-falling), sesquisyllables written with apostrophe; compounds show reduced tonal variation on the left-hand member (p. ~88).
